PMGT1865 Week 05

PMGT1865 Week 05 — Resource Planning

Resources and the Planning Process

Project resources include people, equipment, technology, materials, consumables and finance. Materials are normally consumed, or used up. People and equipment are applied to perform work and may be available for later activities.

Resource management establishes how resources will be estimated, acquired, allocated, managed and used. A schedule based only on logical dependencies can be infeasible if its resource demand exceeds availability.

The resource-planning process has three main steps:

Identify the types and quantities of resources required.

Determine when they are needed and allocate them to scheduled activities.

Decide how to obtain them: Buy externally, Team with partners, or Make using internal capability.

Estimation Approaches

Approach

Meaning and use

Deterministic estimation

Produces a single estimate from stated assumptions, rates or judgements

Probabilistic or stochastic estimation

Represents uncertainty through ranges, distributions or simulation

Parametric estimation

Multiplies a quantity of work by an effort or cost rate, adjusted for context

Analogous estimation

Starts with comparable previous work and adjusts for differences

Bottom-up estimation

Estimates detailed tasks or work packages and aggregates the results

Workload/capacity analysis

Compares required effort with available resource capacity

Historical data and expert judgement

Use previous observations and experienced assessment to inform estimates

Three-point estimating uses optimistic, most likely and pessimistic estimates. Monte Carlo simulation samples uncertain inputs to explore possible outcomes. Vendor bids and Delphi expert consensus can also inform estimates, but do not automatically produce probability distributions: their uncertainty must be explicitly modelled if a probabilistic estimate is required.

Bottom-up estimates can be more detailed and potentially more accurate, but require sufficiently defined tasks and more estimating effort. Method selection depends on available information, uncertainty and the accuracy required.

Effort, Duration and Resource Units

Effort, or work, is the total resource input, measured in units such as person-hours or person-days. Duration is elapsed working time. Resource units describe how much capacity is assigned, such as the number of full-time workers.

For constant capacity and proportional productivity:

• Work = Duration × Resource units.

• Duration = Work ÷ Resource units.

• Adjusted effort per unit = Standard effort per unit ÷ Efficiency factor.

• Total effort = Adjusted effort per unit × Quantity.

The efficiency factor is a dimensionless multiplier relative to standard productivity. At 80% efficiency, each unit requires 1 ÷ 0.80 times the standard effort. When work is measured in person-hours and units are workers, duration is in working hours; conversion to days requires hours worked per day.

These relationships assume that work can be distributed effectively across the assigned resources. Adding people does not always reduce duration proportionally when work is indivisible or coordination requirements increase.

Install 25 turbines. Standard effort is 40 person-hours per turbine; efficiency is 80%. Five labourers work eight hours per day.

Worked Example — Analogous Duration Estimate

A comparable activity took 100 days in the United Kingdom. Assume the Australian context requires 15% more time.

Adjustment = 100 × 0.15 = 15 days.

Adjusted duration = 100 + 15 = 100 × 1.15 = 115 days.

The adjustment is a stated contextual assumption, not a universal location-based rule.

Resource Loading and Histograms

Resource loading allocates resource quantities and rates to scheduled activities. A resource histogram plots the resource demand in each time period, making peaks, troughs and over-allocation visible.

Prepare a logically valid activity schedule.

Assign resource types, quantities, calendars and rates to activities.

Sum each resource's demand for each day or other chosen period.

Plot a separate histogram for each relevant resource type.

Compare demand with period-by-period availability.

Adjust the allocation or schedule and recalculate the demand profile.

Over-allocation occurs when scheduled demand exceeds available capacity in a period. Resource calendars describe availability, including working hours, non-working days and other commitments.

Float, Smoothing and Levelling

Total float is an activity's allowable timing flexibility without delaying the calculated project finish:

Total float = LS − ES = LF − EF.

ES and EF are early start and early finish; LS and LF are late start and late finish. These are obtained from forward and backward network calculations.

Technique

Main objective and implications

Resource smoothing

Reduce peaks and troughs within available float while preserving the required project finish and logical relationships

Resource levelling

Reconcile the schedule with resource limits; may delay or split activities and may extend project duration

Time-constrained or unlimited-resource levelling

Reduce peak resource requirements or associated costs while maintaining the calculated project duration

Resource-constrained or limited-resource levelling

Hold resource capacity to its limit and seek the shortest feasible duration, potentially extending the schedule

A trial-and-adjustment method starts with the schedule, allocates resources on a bar chart, totals demand, draws a histogram, compares availability and moves selected non-critical activities within float. Every adjustment must preserve dependencies. If available float cannot resolve the overload, investigate revised sequencing, splitting where feasible, reassignment or additional capacity.

Worked Example — Resource Utilisation Factor

The Resource Utilisation Factor (RUF) compares planned resource work with capacity over a stated time window. For a resource measured in workers, work is measured in worker-days.

RUF = Planned resource-days ÷ (Capacity level × Days in the window) × 100%.

Here the capacity level is taken to be the peak scheduled resource level, not an independently fixed staffing complement. This measures how fully the rectangular peak-capacity envelope is used. Both cases contain 64 resource-days of work over an 11-day window.

The work and time window remain unchanged, while the peak falls from 11 to 7. The higher RUF indicates a more even demand profile relative to the chosen peak. If actual available capacity is used instead, label it explicitly; it measures utilisation against that capacity rather than against the peak demand.

Linking Resources to Cost

Resource quantities, effort, rates and durations support activity estimates, budgets and a cost baseline, the approved time-phased budget used to compare planned and actual costs.

• Labour cost = Effort × Cost per effort unit.

• Material cost = Quantity × Unit price.

• Time-based equipment cost = Hire duration × Hire rate.

• Add separately applicable fixed costs and other charges without counting costs already included in rates twice.

The estimate should explain whether workers are paid only for productive hours or for complete shifts, and whether rates already include overheads. Resource availability and payment conditions can affect cost even when the technical work quantity is unchanged.

Worked Example — Welding with a Changing Crew

A seam is 150 metres long. Allow 5% additional welding for rework. Standard productivity is 2.5 metres per person-hour, reduced to 85% efficiency. Two welders work eight-hour days for the first four days; three welders are available thereafter. Labour costs $80 per person-hour actually used.

The rounded total effort is 74.12 person-hours. The crew finishes approximately 3.37 hours into the fifth working day. Duration and cost calculations retain full precision until the final result; multiplying the already-rounded 74.12 by $80 would introduce a rounding difference.

Human-Resource Planning and Responsibility Structures

Human-resource planning covers roles and responsibilities, competencies, reporting relationships, staffing calendars, acquisition, training, transition, performance management, conflict resolution and escalation.

An Organisation Breakdown Structure (OBS) shows organisational units, roles and reporting relationships. A Work Breakdown Structure (WBS) decomposes project scope into manageable deliverables and work packages.

A Responsibility Assignment Matrix (RAM) links WBS items with OBS roles or organisational units. It identifies responsibility for each item of work and the other parties involved.

RACI is one form of RAM:

Letter

Role

Meaning

R

Responsible

Performs the work

A

Accountable

Owns approval or sign-off and answerability for the result

C

Consulted

Provides specialist input through two-way communication

I

Informed

Receives progress or outcome information

Each work item needs at least one Responsible party and normally one clearly identified Accountable party. Use Consulted and Informed selectively so the matrix clarifies communication rather than distributing every role to everyone.
